title: Multiplicative-to-unipotent vanishing over every base algebra
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field]. All groups are affine $k$-group schemes [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], and subgroups are closed subgroup schemes [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Unipotent means admitting a closed group immersion [def-weil-closed-immersion] into some $\mathcal U_{n,k}\subseteq\operatorname{GL}_{n,k}$, $n\geq1$ [def-sc-general-linear-group], where $\mathcal U_{n,k}(A)$ consists of upper triangular matrices with diagonal entries $1$ for every commutative $k$-algebra $A$. A group is of multiplicative type if after extension to an algebraic closure of $k$ it admits a closed subgroup inclusion into $\mathbf G_m^r$ for some $r\geq0$ [def-sfb-tori-multiplicative-type, def-weil-algebraic-closure, def-sc-gm-ga]. Let $D$ be of multiplicative type and let $U$ be unipotent. For every commutative $k$-algebra $R$, every homomorphism of $R$-group schemes $f:D_R\to U_R$ is trivial. Scalar extension here means fibre product with $\operatorname{Spec}R$ [def-pc-base-change, def-weil-affine-spectrum]. Equivalently, for every commutative $R$-algebra $A$ and every $d\in D_R(A)$, one has $f_A(d)=1$. Neither $R$ nor $A$ is required to be reduced, and neither group is required to be smooth or connected.

source.place: Proposition 15.18, printed p.312; Theorem 14.5, pp.281--282, for the unitriangular meaning of unipotent.

proof.text: Put $K=\bar k$ and $S=R\otimes_kK$. The map $R\to S$ is faithfully flat by [lem-weil-pbc-field-extension-base-change-faithfully-flat]. By [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-product-affine-spectra], scalar extension of the affine schemes and their maps is tensor extension of their coordinate algebras. For $B=\Gamma(D_R,\mathcal O)$, [lem-weil-pbc-faithfully-flat-universally-injective] makes $B\to B\otimes_RS$ injective. Consequently two maps from the coordinate algebra of $U_R$ to $B$ are equal if their scalar extensions to $S$ are equal: subtract their values on each element and use this injection. The uniqueness assertion in [def-weil-affine-spectrum] then implies equality of the corresponding scheme morphisms. Thus it suffices to show that $f_S$ is the identity-valued morphism. If $R$ is the zero ring this conclusion also holds, since all the coordinate algebras after base change are zero.

source.place: Proposition 15.18, p.312, conclusion; elementary faithfully flat scalar-extension reduction added by the worker.

proof.text: By the multiplicative-type hypothesis $D_K$ is a closed subgroup of $\mathbf G_{m,K}^r$. Apply [lem-sfb-split-torus-subgroups-diagonalizable] over the algebraically closed field $K$: there is a finitely generated abelian group $M$ with $D_K\simeq\operatorname{Spec}K[M]$, with basis $e_m$ and coproduct $e_m\mapsto e_m\otimes e_m$. Extending from $K$ to $S$, [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-product-affine-spectra] identifies its coordinate ring with $S\otimes_KK[M]=S[M]$. Explicitly $s\otimes\sum_m a_me_m\mapsto\sum_m(sa_m)e_m$ has inverse $\sum_m s_me_m\mapsto\sum_m s_m\otimes e_m$; the tensor relations show these are inverse ring maps, preserving the displayed coproduct. Hence $D_S=D_S(M)$ with exactly the operations in [def-sfb-ring-diagonalizable-group]. No assertion about geometric points is used in this identification.

source.place: Theorems 12.8 and 12.9(c), pp.233--234; explicit scalar extension of their group-algebra description.

proof.text: For any commutative ring $S$, a primitive element $z=\sum_m a_me_m\in S[M]$ is zero. Indeed, apply the two coefficient projections at $m$ to $\Delta z=z\otimes1+1\otimes z$, using the coproduct of [def-sfb-ring-diagonalizable-group]. For $m\ne0$, the coefficient at $(m,m)$ gives $a_m=0$; the coefficient at $(0,0)$ gives $a_0=2a_0$, hence $a_0=0$ by subtraction. These projections are $S$-linear, so their tensor product evaluates the equality in $S\otimes_SS=S$; no domain assumption is involved. A group morphism $h:D_S(M)\to\mathbf G_{a,S}$ has coordinate map $S[t]\to S[M]$. By [def-sc-gm-ga] and the affine-product identification [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-product-affine-spectra], its multiplication compatibility is precisely $\Delta h^*(t)=h^*(t)\otimes1+1\otimes h^*(t)$. Thus $h^*(t)=0$, and [def-weil-affine-spectrum] says $h$ is the zero homomorphism. This proves additive vanishing over the entire ring $S$, including its nilpotents.

source.place: Proposition 15.18, p.312, additive vanishing input; direct coefficient proof supplied by the worker using the Hopf algebra of Theorem 12.8, p.233.

proof.text: Choose the given closed group immersion $U\hookrightarrow\mathcal U_{n,k}$. Apply [lem-sfb-unitriangular-coordinate-filtration] to this unitriangular group: $U^{(0)}=\mathcal U_n$, $U^{(m)}=1$, and $p_r:U^{(r-1)}\to\mathbf G_a$ has scheme-theoretic kernel $U^{(r)}$, where $m=n(n-1)/2$. Base change these diagrams to $S$. The universal property of [def-pc-fibre-product], with [def-pc-base-change], identifies the new kernels with $U^{(r)}_S$: both are the same iterated fibre product along the identity section. Inductively construct group morphisms $g_r:D_S(M)\to U^{(r)}_S$ through which $g_0=(U_S\hookrightarrow\mathcal U_{n,S})\circ f_S$ factors. The base $g_0$ is given. If $g_{r-1}$ is constructed, Step 3 makes $p_{r,S}g_{r-1}$ zero. The kernel fibre-product property gives a unique factor $g_r$. It is a group morphism because its composite with the kernel inclusion preserves multiplication and the inclusion is injective on points (it is the zero locus of the first $r$ coordinates). This gives the induction step. At $r=m$ the target is $1$, so $g_0$ is trivial; when $n=1$ this is already the base case.

source.place: Example 6.49(a)--(c), pp.136--137, unitriangular filtration; Proposition 15.18, p.312, reduction to additive homomorphisms, realized by this finite induction.

proof.text: For every commutative $S$-algebra $A$, the original closed subgroup inclusion $U(A)\hookrightarrow\mathcal U_n(A)$ is injective by [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Base change has the same points on $S$-algebras. Step 4 therefore gives $f_{S,A}(d)=1$ for every $d\in D_S(A)$, so $f_S$ is the trivial morphism. Step 1 descends its equality with the identity-valued morphism to $R$. The asserted formula on every $R$-algebra $A$ follows by evaluating this equality. All coefficient comparisons and subgroup injections were made on all algebra-valued points, so no reducedness, smoothness or connectedness was imposed.

source.place: Proposition 15.18, p.312, final conclusion; cancellation of the given subgroup immersion and the scalar-extension reduction of Step 1.

proof_origin.place: Proposition 15.18, p.312, proved here by a group-algebra coefficient calculation and the filtration of Example 6.49, pp.136--137, instead of the source's rational-cohomology proof.
